title: Infected TAVI prosthesis explantation and bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement

questions.question: What is shown before the operation begins?
options: Preparation for a high-risk cardiac reoperation
questions.explanation: The opening minute shows the operative team and preparation before the chest is opened.

questions.question: What procedure is announced at the start of the video?
options: Explantation of an infected TAVI prosthesis followed by bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement
questions.explanation: The planned operation is removal of the infected transcatheter valve and replacement with a surgical bioprosthetic aortic valve.

questions.question: What is the first incision shown?
options: A skin incision for access to the chest
questions.explanation: The team begins with the skin incision that leads toward the median sternotomy.

questions.question: What does the saw separate during the early exposure?
questions.explanation: The surgeon uses the saw to perform a sternotomy and open the chest.

questions.question: Why is heparin administered before bypass?
options: To prevent clotting in the cardiopulmonary bypass circuit
questions.explanation: Heparin prevents coagulation when blood contacts the artificial surfaces of the bypass circuit.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of the chest retractor in this phase?
options: To improve exposure of the mediastinal operative field
questions.explanation: The retractor spreads the sternum so the pericardium and heart can be accessed safely.

questions.question: What do pericardial stay sutures provide?
options: Stable retraction of the pericardial edges
questions.explanation: Stay sutures hold the pericardium open and stabilize the operative field.

questions.question: Why does the surgeon palpate the TAVI frame before the aortotomy?
options: To choose a safe level for opening the aorta
questions.explanation: Palpating the frame identifies its height and incorporation so the aortotomy can be planned around it.

questions.question: What is being assessed when the aortic tissue is described as thin?
options: The tissue's ability to hold cannulation sutures
The diameter of the prosthetic leaflets
questions.explanation: Thin or fragile aortic tissue may not tolerate concentrated traction, so the cannulation sutures must distribute force.

questions.question: What does the aortic cannulation suture help secure?
questions.explanation: The purse-string suture controls the arterial entry site and limits bleeding around the aortic cannula.

questions.question: Which two cannulation preparations are emphasized?
options: Venous cannulation and antegrade cardioplegia cannulation
questions.explanation: The team prepares the venous cannula site and the site for antegrade cardioplegia.

questions.question: What is the immediate concern when advancing a cannula through a thin aorta?
options: Avoiding wall injury and a cannulation leak
questions.explanation: A thin aortic wall can dissect or bleed if the cannula is advanced aggressively.

questions.question: What is the purpose of evacuating air from the lines before bypass?
options: To reduce the risk of air entering the circulation
questions.explanation: The team empties and de-airs the line before delivering fluid and starting bypass.

questions.question: What does an activated clotting time above four hundred seconds indicate here?
questions.explanation: The team waits for a high ACT before going on pump to reduce circuit thrombosis risk.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the left atrial vent suture after bypass begins?
options: To permit decompression and removal of blood or air from the left heart
questions.explanation: The left atrial vent helps keep the field bloodless and assists de-airing later.

questions.question: Which structure must be avoided when placing the retrograde cardioplegia purse string?
questions.explanation: The surgeon identifies the right coronary artery near the intended site and avoids injuring it.

questions.question: Why is the right atrium kept filled while the retrograde cannula is inserted?
options: To reduce the risk of air entering and air-locking the venous line
To prevent the aorta from calcifying
questions.explanation: An empty atrium can entrain air into the venous drainage system.

questions.question: What could happen if the retrograde cannula is advanced too far?
options: The bypass circuit would gain oxygen
Perfusion of the right coronary territory could be reduced
questions.explanation: The video warns that an overly deep cannula can further compromise right coronary perfusion.

questions.question: Why is the plane between the aorta and pulmonary artery developed?
options: To create a safer corridor for the aortotomy
questions.explanation: The dissection separates adjacent structures before the aorta is opened.

questions.question: What is used to arrest and protect the heart after the cross clamp?
questions.explanation: The heart is arrested with cold cardioplegia delivered retrogradely after cross clamping.

questions.question: Through which route is the vent cannula placed into the left atrium?
options: Through the right superior pulmonary vein
questions.explanation: The vent passes through the right superior pulmonary vein into the left atrium.

questions.question: What is the main technical problem when the TAVI frame is embedded?
options: It must be removed through the femoral vein
It must be exposed and dissected without forceful traction
It must be inflated like a balloon
It must be left in place
questions.explanation: The surgeon exposes the frame and avoids pulling until the adherent areas are controlled.

questions.question: What complication occurs while separating the noncoronary stabilization arch?
options: An injury to the inner layer of the aortic wall
questions.explanation: The video reports an inner-layer aortic injury that will later be reinforced with a Teflon patch.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the snare technique during TAVI explantation?
options: To gain controlled purchase on the stent frame and progressively collapse it
questions.explanation: Sutures passed through the frame allow controlled traction and reduction of the prosthesis.

questions.question: What should happen to infected prosthetic material removed from the field?
options: It should be sent promptly for microbiologic culture
It should be returned to the bypass reservoir
It should be placed in the sternum
It should be used as a pledget
questions.explanation: The surgeon removes contaminated material and sends it to microbiology.

questions.question: What is done while the final snare sutures are placed?
options: Retrograde cardioplegia is continued to protect the arrested heart
questions.explanation: The final snare sutures are placed while cardioplegia continues to protect the myocardium.

questions.question: What abnormality of the TAVI frame is noted during explantation?
options: The frame is made of bone
The frame has migrated into the mitral valve
questions.explanation: Underexpanded segments are identified and require additional sutures for controlled removal.

questions.question: Why are the sutures gathered and tightened gradually?
options: To reduce the frame while limiting sudden traction on fragile tissue
questions.explanation: Gradual tightening is a controlled way to mobilize a tissue-integrated prosthesis.

questions.question: What happens after several sutures snap?
options: The team changes the angle and follows a remaining plane of separation
It immediately implants the new valve
questions.explanation: The team adapts by approaching from a visible tissue plane rather than applying uncontrolled force.

questions.question: What makes the dissection especially difficult in this phase?
options: Dense superior adhesions between the frame and aortic tissue
questions.explanation: The surgeon repeatedly identifies areas of dense adhesion that require careful sharp dissection.

questions.question: What happens when the hematocrit is eighteen?
options: One unit of packed red blood cells is transfused
questions.explanation: The team responds to the low hematocrit with packed red cell transfusion.

questions.question: What important fact about TAVI explains why native valve tissue is still present?
options: The native valve is always removed first
TAVI replaces only the mitral valve
The transcatheter prosthesis is deployed within the calcified native valve
questions.explanation: TAVI generally compresses the native leaflets rather than excising them, so they remain within the device and wall complex.

questions.question: Why is a rongeur used selectively during native valve and tissue removal?
options: To remove selected tissue while preserving viable aortic wall
questions.explanation: The surgeon distinguishes loose or removable material from tissue that should remain for repair.

questions.question: Why is the annulus cleaned before the new bioprosthesis is implanted?
options: To remove calcium and debris that could impair seating or embolize
To increase the size of the sternum
questions.explanation: A clean annulus supports proper seating and reduces residual infectious or embolic material.

questions.question: Why does the surgeon avoid excessive debridement near the commissure?
options: The region is outside the heart
The region is used for bone wax
The region is close to the conduction system and fragile aortic tissue
The region contains the femoral artery
questions.explanation: Near the commissure, preserving tissue can reduce structural injury and conduction disturbance.

questions.question: What marks the transition from contaminated explantation to the clean reconstruction phase?
options: Copious irrigation, instrument separation, and glove change
questions.explanation: The team irrigates, separates contaminated instruments, and changes gloves before reconstruction.

questions.question: What is the purpose of copious saline irrigation?
options: To remove residual tissue and calcific debris that could embolize
questions.explanation: Irrigation and suction clear debris from the left ventricle, annulus, and coronary ostia.

questions.question: Which sizer is ultimately selected for the surgical valve?
questions.explanation: The twenty-one millimetre sizer seats well, so the team does not force a larger valve.

questions.question: Where are the pledgets placed for the new bioprosthetic valve?
options: On the ventricular side of the annulus
questions.explanation: The pledgets are placed on the ventricular side to distribute suture tension.

questions.question: What suture distribution is described while preparing the valve?
options: Ten-ten, only at the coronary ostia
questions.explanation: The surgeon describes a three-four-four distribution while excluding the commissural positions.

questions.question: Why is a twenty-one millimetre surgical valve chosen instead of a larger one?
options: The larger valve could injure fragile tissue or the conduction system
The larger valve would not contain leaflets
The larger valve cannot be sterilized
The larger valve is a venous cannula
questions.explanation: The video explicitly links forcing a larger valve with injury and a higher heart-block risk.

questions.question: Why is retrograde cardioplegia given before lowering the new valve?
options: To protect the myocardium and flush the coronary circulation
questions.explanation: The dose maintains myocardial protection and can flush the coronary circulation in reverse.

questions.question: What is checked while the valve is rotated and the commissural sutures are released?
options: That the mitral annulus is calcified
That the prosthesis remains aligned with the planned commissures
questions.explanation: The valve is rotated and released in a controlled sequence so its commissures and sutures remain aligned.

questions.question: What is the benefit of reverse coronary flushing during cardioplegia?
options: It can help clear residual debris while protecting the myocardium
questions.explanation: Retrograde cardioplegia protects the heart and can flush the coronary circulation in reverse.

questions.question: What is the main task while the remaining valve sutures are tied?
options: Keep the prosthesis aligned and secure while maintaining myocardial protection
questions.explanation: The valve must remain correctly positioned while the final sutures are tied during arrest.

questions.question: Why is additional retrograde cardioplegia given during the prolonged implant?
options: To maintain myocardial protection during the cross-clamp interval
questions.explanation: Repeated doses reduce myocardial oxygen demand while the reconstruction continues.

questions.question: What is confirmed during the later coronary ostia assessment?
options: The prosthesis is not occluding the coronary ostia
questions.explanation: The surgeon confirms that the coronary openings remain unobstructed.

questions.question: What is the main task during aortotomy closure?
options: Create a secure, hemostatic closure around the repaired aortic wall
questions.explanation: The aortotomy is closed with sutures while the team maintains myocardial protection.

questions.question: Why are lung inflation and Trendelenburg positioning used before clamp removal?
options: They help displace and evacuate residual intracardiac air
questions.explanation: Filling the lungs and using a head-down position are part of deliberate de-airing.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the aortic root vent during de-airing?
options: To suction residual air and fluid from the root
questions.explanation: Root vent suction helps remove air before the heart ejects.

questions.question: What is being controlled while the heart and aorta are filled before clamp removal?
options: Residual air and the level of cardiac filling
questions.explanation: The team fills the heart carefully and keeps suction active while removing remaining air.

questions.question: What is done as the aortotomy is tied and the clamp removal approaches?
options: Gentle root venting and temporary carotid compression are prepared
questions.explanation: The team prepares a controlled de-airing maneuver before removing the clamp.

questions.question: What does the team do immediately after the cross clamp is removed?
options: Maintain venting, release the carotids, and assess rhythm and filling
questions.explanation: The transition to reperfusion includes controlled venting, release of carotid compression, and rhythm assessment.

questions.question: How is a small aortotomy bleeding point reinforced?
options: With bone wax inside the annulus
questions.explanation: The surgeon places pledgets to spread tension across fragile aortic tissue.

questions.question: What rhythm complication is specifically assessed after the heart starts beating?
questions.explanation: The team assesses atrioventricular synchrony and checks for heart block after annular surgery.

questions.question: What finding supports a gradual separation from bypass?
options: Good contractility with no evidence of heart block
questions.explanation: The team reports good contraction and no block before reducing support.

questions.question: What happens when the pacemaker is turned on?
questions.explanation: The pacing wire is tested and capture is confirmed.

questions.question: How is cardiopulmonary bypass reduced near the end?
options: The heart is left empty permanently
Flow is tapered stepwise while vents and cannulas are removed
The pump is stopped before filling the heart
The arterial cannula is removed first without pressure checks
questions.explanation: The team fills the heart and reduces flow gradually before removing the vents and cannulas.

questions.question: What medication is started to reverse the effect of heparin?
questions.explanation: Protamine is started after bypass to reverse heparin, with blood pressure monitored during decannulation.

questions.question: What is checked in the final inspection?
options: The sternum before it is opened
Hemostasis and stability of the repaired area
questions.explanation: The final inspection confirms satisfactory clot formation and a stable repair.

questions.question: What does the public study pack emphasize in the closing segment?
options: The operative sequence, safety checks, and staged recovery from bypass
A new infection requiring another valve
A second sternotomy for the same operation
A medication prescription for home use
questions.explanation: The pack emphasizes the observed operative sequence and safety checks; it is educational surgical commentary, not a personal treatment plan.

questions.question: Which sequence best summarizes the operation?
options: Sternal closure without removing the infected valve
Infected TAVI explantation, debridement and irrigation, surgical bioprosthetic replacement, de-airing, and staged weaning from bypass
Mitral repair followed by carotid stenting only
Immediate prosthesis extraction without bypass or reconstruction
questions.explanation: The operation combines source control, removal of the native valve and infected TAVI, new valve implantation, de-airing, and controlled recovery.

narration.text: This is a real high risk redo operation viewed from the surgeon's field. The educational thread is source control for prosthetic infection, safe removal of a transcatheter valve, and replacement with a surgical bioprosthesis. The video is graphic operative footage, so use the commentary to track decisions rather than memorizing isolated movements.

The planned procedure is explantation of an infected TAVI prosthesis followed by bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement. Infection changes the objective from simply correcting valve function to removing infected foreign material, controlling contamination, and reconstructing a safe annulus for a new valve.

The operation begins with a skin incision. This is the access phase of a median sternotomy, and it must preserve orientation and hemostasis before the sternum is opened. In a redo cardiac operation, tissue planes may be less predictable, so controlled dissection is part of the safety strategy.

The oscillating saw divides the sternum to create the central exposure. The saw is kept in the bone while the team protects the structures beneath it. Once the chest is open, the team can expose the pericardium and prepare for cardiopulmonary bypass.

Heparin is administered before the bypass circuit is used because blood contacting the artificial surfaces would otherwise clot. The team also evaluates the exposed tissues and controls cancellous sternal bleeding. Adequate anticoagulation is checked later with the activated clotting time.

The retractor spreads the sternum and improves access. Bone wax can reduce bleeding from cut bone, while the bypass lines are organized for the next phase. Clear line management matters because the arterial, venous, vent, and cardioplegia circuits each have a different job.

The pericardium is opened and stay sutures bring its edges into a stable position. This exposes the heart without pulling directly on it. The stays also help maintain a controlled operative field while the team identifies the implanted frame and plans cannulation.

The surgeon palpates the TAVI frame before making the aortotomy. The frame is not very high, but part of it has become incorporated into the aortic wall. Locating the stent by touch helps choose an incision that gives access while preserving as much healthy aorta as possible.

The aortic tissue is assessed before cannulation. Tissue quality determines how firmly a purse string can hold and how much traction the wall can tolerate. The team now places the sutures that will secure the arterial and venous cannulas for bypass.

The aortic cannulation suture creates a controlled entry site for arterial perfusion. A snare around the purse string can tighten the tissue around the cannula and limit bleeding. In fragile aortic tissue, the suture must be wide enough to distribute force.

Venous cannulation and the antegrade cardioplegia site are prepared. The venous line drains the right heart to the pump, while the cardioplegia cannula later delivers solution to arrest and protect the myocardium. Each purse string is placed with its final cannula path in mind.

The aorta is described as thin, so the arterial cannula is advanced carefully. A secure cannula must deliver flow without dissecting the wall or producing a leak. The goal is a stable connection that will remain reliable when full pump flow begins.

The team evacuates air and checks the lines before starting bypass. The flow is reduced briefly and the arterial pressure falls to about eighty over thirty-five. An activated clotting time above four hundred seconds confirms strong heparinization for the bypass circuit.

Cardiopulmonary bypass begins and unloads the heart. A left atrial vent suture is placed so blood and air can be removed from the left side. At the same time, the team plans retrograde cardioplegia through the coronary sinus.

The retrograde cannulation site is chosen at a prominent point while avoiding the right coronary artery. The purse string is deliberately wider than the cannula. This gives room for the cannula and helps prevent bleeding when it is secured.

The right coronary artery is kept in mind while the aortic root and retrograde cannulas are positioned. The team expects that the heart could fibrillate during insertion, so cardioplegia must be ready before the cannula enters.

The right atrium is kept filled while the retrograde cannula is guided. If the atrium collapses, air can enter the venous line and create an air lock. The cannula is brought anterior to the venous cannula and guided manually toward the coronary sinus.

The cannula is advanced by feel along the atrioventricular groove. A syringe is used to judge balloon firmness without overinflating it. Advancing too far could reduce perfusion to the right coronary territory, which is already less reliably supplied by retrograde cardioplegia.

The plane between the aorta and pulmonary artery is developed before the aortotomy. This separation creates a safer working corridor and reduces the chance of injuring adjacent structures. The cross clamp and root vent are then prepared for cardiac arrest.

Cold saline and retrograde cardioplegia are used after the cross clamp is applied. The infected field is treated as contaminated, so instruments that enter it will later be removed. Severe aortic regurgitation explains why antegrade root delivery is unreliable and retrograde delivery is emphasized.

A vent passes through the right superior pulmonary vein into the left atrium. It keeps the field relatively bloodless and later helps evacuate intracardiac air. The aorta is opened at the planned level, and the metal struts of the TAVI frame become visible.

The prosthesis is embedded, so the surgeon exposes it before applying traction. Strong suction keeps the left atrial side decompressed. The upper crowns of the frame are identified, but one region is deeply incorporated and requires sharp, controlled dissection.

The noncoronary stabilization arch is densely adherent to the aortic wall. Separation produces an injury in the inner aortic layer, so the plan is to reinforce the area with a Teflon patch during closure. The whole prosthesis appears infected, making complete source control essential.

The snare technique uses sutures passed through the stent frame to control and progressively collapse the prosthesis. Milrinone is started while the team maintains myocardial support. This is a useful example of how explantation combines mechanical control with careful perfusion management.

Visible infected material is removed and sent for culture. It is handled as contaminated and kept from falling into the heart. Sterility remains critical even though the operation is already dealing with infection; every additional fragment or contaminated instrument can increase the burden of source control.

Retrograde cardioplegia is restarted while the final snare sutures are placed. The prosthesis is held under controlled traction rather than forceful pulling. The aim is to reduce the frame while protecting the aortic wall and the adjacent annulus.

Several portions of the TAVI frame never fully expanded. Underexpansion can leave abnormal surfaces and disturbed flow, and it can make later explantation more difficult. The surgeon passes additional sutures through the struts to obtain a controlled purchase on the frame.

The sutures are gathered and tightened gradually. The team notes that inflammation extends through an underexpanded region. The sequence shows why explantation is not a simple extraction: the frame, native valve, and aortic wall may be joined by fibrosis and infection.

Cold saline is poured over the prosthesis while the sutures are tightened. Several sutures snap, so the team changes its angle and searches for a remaining plane of separation. When a planned maneuver fails, following an existing tissue plane can be safer than adding force.

The surgeon lifts and dissects the prosthesis from superior adhesions. The frame is separated step by step, with suction and sharp instruments used close to the adherent tissue. The purpose is to free the device while preserving enough aortic tissue for reconstruction.

This minute remains focused on dense adherence. Gentle movement toward a safer direction lets the surgeon continue the dissection without tearing the wall. The visible difficulty is a reminder that chronic implantation can convert a transcatheter device into a tissue-integrated surgical problem.

The critical area has very poor aortic tissue and one remaining point still holds the prosthesis. The hematocrit is eighteen, so a unit of packed red cells is transfused. Hemostasis and oxygen-carrying capacity matter during a prolonged, high-risk bypass procedure.

The prosthesis is described as infected throughout its interior and is sent to microbiology. The native aortic valve is then removed. During TAVI, the calcified native leaflets are not excised; the transcatheter prosthesis is deployed within them, leaving native tissue compressed between the device and aortic wall.

The absence of an aortic root abscess is favorable, but the tissue is still fragile. A rongeur and fine forceps remove selected material while the surgeon distinguishes loose debris from tissue that is still attached. Preserving viable wall is as important as removing infection.

Before implanting the new valve, the annulus must be clean of calcific tissue. Residual calcium or infected debris can prevent seating, impair sealing, or become an embolic source. Cardioplegia is also given through the right coronary ostium to maintain myocardial protection.

The surgeon emphasizes that myocardial protection must be adequate for successful separation from bypass. The final infected areas are close to a commissure and the conduction system, so tissue is removed selectively. An overly aggressive debridement could create structural damage or heart block.

The team preserves a small adherent area and plans a fine internal repair rather than removing more tissue. The contaminated instruments are separated, gloves are changed, and the clean phase begins. The mitral valve is inspected for extension of endocarditis and no extension is seen.

Copious saline irrigation and suction clear the left ventricle and aortic annulus. The goal is to remove tissue fragments and calcific debris that could embolize. The coronary ostia are flushed, and clean drapes and instruments mark the transition to reconstruction.

Annular sizers are tested at twenty-five, twenty-three, and twenty-one millimetres. The twenty-one millimetre sizer seats well, so the team chooses it rather than forcing a larger valve. Sizing is a balance between hemodynamics, fragile tissue, coronary anatomy, and the conduction system.

A twenty-one millimetre bioprosthesis is selected and placed in a supra-annular position. Pledgets sit on the ventricular side of the annulus to spread suture tension. A larger valve could injure fragile tissue or the conduction system, increasing the risk of bleeding or heart block.

The team spaces the annular sutures in a three-four-four pattern while excluding the commissures. Even distribution helps the sewing ring sit symmetrically. In a small or damaged annulus, suture geometry is part of valve function and part of the protection against paravalvular leakage.

The new valve is twenty-one millimetres because a twenty-five millimetre surgical valve could not be seated safely. The earlier transcatheter valve had been twenty-five millimetres but remained underexpanded. The discussion also identifies a high-velocity jet as a predisposing flow disturbance for endocarditis.

The commissural sutures are positioned with small adjustments to compensate for unequal spacing. Before the valve is lowered, retrograde cardioplegia is given and the coronary ostia are flushed. This protects the myocardium and helps clear any residual material from the coronary circulation.

Retrograde cardioplegia provides myocardial protection while the valve is being seated. Reverse flow through the coronary circulation can also help wash out debris. The valve is rotated so its commissures align with the planned suture distribution.

The valve is being lowered and the commissural sutures are released in sequence. The conversation briefly turns to cerebral protection, but the operative principle remains the same: protect vital organs while maintaining a stable, bloodless field during reconstruction.

The remaining sutures are brought through and tied while the valve stays aligned. Additional cardioplegia is used when needed. Maintaining arrest during the final seating and tying phase limits myocardial oxygen demand while the new prosthesis is secured.

Another retrograde dose is administered. Re-dosing cardioplegia is a way to maintain myocardial protection during a prolonged cross-clamp interval. The team keeps the field controlled and continues the final annular sutures rather than rushing the reconstruction.

Retrograde cardioplegia is used again and the surgeon checks the coronary ostia. The ostia remain open and are not being obstructed by the prosthesis. This is a key anatomic safety check before closing the aorta and restoring forward coronary flow.

The suture ends are shortened and the aortotomy closure begins. The closure must restore a watertight aortic wall while incorporating the area that was injured during explantation. The team continues cardioplegia until the repair is secure.

Suction is placed inside the aorta and rewarming begins. The surgeon feels the tissue as the needle passes, using resistance as a practical assessment of wall integrity. The team avoids removing a surface that looks covered but is not clearly nonviable.

Warm saline, lung inflation, and a slight Trendelenburg position prepare the heart for de-airing. Air left in the left heart could be ejected to the coronary or cerebral circulation when the heart beats, so removal is deliberately performed before the clamp comes off.

Residual air is evacuated from the heart and aorta while the chambers are filled in a controlled way. A head-down position helps direct bubbles away from the cerebral circulation. Venting and gentle suction continue until the team is satisfied with the de-airing.

The aortotomy is nearly tied and the team uses gentle root-vent suction while preparing to remove the clamp. Brief carotid compression is requested as an additional maneuver during de-airing. The aim is to minimize the chance that residual bubbles reach the brain.

The cross clamp is removed with the aortic root and left atrial vents active. The carotids are released, amiodarone is given, and the heart is kept decompressed while rhythm and filling are assessed. This is the transition from protected arrest to reperfusion.

A small bleeding point along the aortotomy is repaired with Teflon pledget-reinforced sutures. The pledget spreads the load over fragile tissue. Temporary pacing settings and vent function are checked at the same time because rhythm and de-airing both affect safe recovery.

The heart has started beating and ventilation resumes. The team assesses atrioventricular synchrony and looks specifically for heart block, an important risk after work near the aortic annulus and conduction tissue. Good pressure and synchrony support a gradual separation from bypass.

Contractility is described as good and there is no evidence of heart block. The aortic root vent remains stronger than the left atrial vent while volume is returned. A pacing wire is placed as a precaution, and urine output is followed as a marker of perfusion.

The pacing wire is adjusted and the team prepares to fill the heart. A functioning pacemaker provides backup while the heart transitions to its own output. The sequence remains incremental: fill, observe pressure and rhythm, then reduce mechanical support.

The pacemaker captures, the heart is filled, and the left atrial vent is removed. Pump flow is reduced stepwise and the remaining vents and root cannula are withdrawn. Gradual reduction allows the team to see whether the new valve and myocardium are tolerating independent circulation.

Cardiopulmonary bypass is terminated and the venous cannula is removed. Protamine is started to reverse heparin, while blood pressure determines when the arterial cannula can safely come out. Decannulation is performed only after the circulation is stable enough to tolerate each step.

The final inspection shows satisfactory clot formation and a stable repaired area. The operation has moved from infection control and device explantation to hemostasis and recovery. This public study pack keeps its commentary focused on the operative technique and its safety checks.

The closing message is the sequence: infected TAVI prosthesis explantation, removal of the native valve, meticulous debridement and irrigation, surgical bioprosthetic replacement, de-airing, and staged separation from bypass. This is an educational operative record, not a guide for self-treatment or a prediction for any individual patient.
